routes.description: Establish resurrection as a plausible cumulative explanation of the early appearances, unexpected resurrection belief, subsequent Christian expansion, and continuing visions.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the historical lines jointly fit Jesus's resurrection and continuing agency more specifically than the proposed ordinary or comparative explanations.

motionBridge.description: The combined historical lines must make Jesus's resurrection a plausible explanation of the motion's specified phenomena.

centralBridges.description: Early individual and group appearance traditions must provide positive evidence that Jesus was encountered alive after death.
The immediate claim of an individually resurrected Messiah must require explanation beyond available Jewish postmortem categories.
Christianity's expansion must connect specifically to the mission and continuing agency attributed to the risen Jesus.
Later cross-cultural Jesus visions must constitute an additional phenomenon consistent with his continuing activity.

subsidiaryBridges.description: No single evidential line must bear the entire case; the lines must retain cumulative relevance when considered together.
Christian appearance and vision reports must be distinguishable from proposed parallels by their attestation, unexpectedness, or cross-cultural pattern.

routes.description: Account for the appearance beliefs, resurrection interpretation, Christian expansion, and later visions without treating a physical resurrection as the probable historical explanation.
routes.successCriteria: Show that source limitations, ordinary experiential mechanisms, cultural interpretation, religious growth, and comparative cases block the resurrection inference.

motionBridge.description: The available historical evidence must remain insufficient to prefer a unique physical resurrection over ordinary or historically comparable explanations.

centralBridges.description: The appearance evidence must be constrained by indirect testimony, sparse descriptions, and uncertainty about the reported witnesses.
Experiences and apocalyptic Jewish beliefs must supply a nonresurrection route to sincere claims that Jesus had been raised.
Religious expansion and fulfilled-mission claims must not establish what happened physically to Jesus's body.
Later Jesus dreams and visions must remain explainable through phenomena also reported in other religious traditions.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Historical inference must compare probabilities without assuming either that miracles are impossible or that testimony establishes them.
Standards applied to Christian testimony must also be applied to Mormon, Marian, and ancient appearance traditions.

sections.title: Early appearance testimony and comparative attestation
sections.rationale: The quality, number, and comparative force of the earliest reported witnesses form the principal evidential link between postmortem experiences and resurrection.

sections.title: Unexpected messianic claim and Jewish interpretive categories
sections.rationale: The origin of belief in an already resurrected Messiah determines whether the claim itself points beyond ordinary experience or follows from available cultural interpretation.

sections.title: Cumulative fit and historical probability
sections.rationale: The motion ultimately turns on whether several converging facts can make resurrection plausible despite the methodological difficulty of inferring a singular physical event.

sections.title: Christian expansion and the worldwide mission claim
sections.rationale: Christianity's historical reach matters only if its scale or fulfillment of an attributed mission bears specifically on resurrection rather than merely recording successful belief.

sections.title: Later visions and cross-religious parallels
sections.rationale: Post-apostolic dreams and visions provide an additional proposed evidential line whose relevance depends on whether they indicate continuing agency or generic religious experience.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Early Pauline sources are used to organize a cumulative case from Jesus's crucifixion, the unexpected resurrection claim, reported appearances, and Christianity's subsequent spread.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly invites Justin Bass to summarize his positive case, and the uninterrupted answer follows that invitation.

response.rationale: This is a constructive move establishing the proposed cumulative route, so no earlier opposing move requires a response.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly organizes several central evidential lines into one route.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative proposition and its component historical claims are readily recoverable, though the inferential standard remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move proposes cumulative evidential force but does not yet compare the components with serious rival explanations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The cumulative structure is coherent, but the independence and combination of the evidential lines are only implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Early Pauline tradition is identified, but several component facts and the cumulative warrant are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly frames the cumulative resurrection explanation required by the pro motion bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive overview does not meaningfully characterize a developed opposing interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies crucifixion, the novel resurrection claim, appearances in 1 Corinthians 15, and subsequent spread.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Reports concerning Paul, Peter, James, Mary Magdalene, groups of disciples, and the five hundred form an early witness tradition offered as positive evidence of Jesus's resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator directly asks Justin Bass to present the appearance evidence, and the sustained first-person exposition answers that request.

response.rationale: This is a constructive presentation of the appearance witnesses and therefore has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly supplies the principal witnesses supporting the appearance line.

precisionFindings.rationale: The witness list is clear, but direct testimony, reported belief, and Gospel narration are not consistently distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker acknowledges uncertainty about Mary but gives limited attention to source dependence and testimonial distance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Multiple reported experiences can support the inference, but the bridge from reports to an encountered risen Jesus remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Several early names and traditions are supplied, while directness, independence, and the five hundred remain insufficiently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the individual and group appearance material required by the central bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents positive witness material without developing a rival account requiring a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt names Peter, James, Paul, Mary Magdalene, disciple groups, and the five hundred as an early tradition.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Only Paul directly attests his own experience, while claims concerning Peter, James, Mary, and the five hundred depend on indirect testimony and require comparison with other religions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests Bart Ehrman's assessment, and the answer is marked by his discussion of historical source evaluation and comparative religious evidence.

components.text: Whether the listed witnesses provide sufficiently direct and independently accessible testimony.
Whether the appearance component supplies secure positive evidence within the cumulative case.
Whether the five hundred and Mary are documented with the same security as Paul.

response.rationale: The reply identifies the source-level defect: only Paul directly records his experience, while other named cases are mediated or uncertain, reducing their evidential force.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly attacks the decisive testimonial premise and states why the witness list overstates accessible attestation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinctions among Paul's direct report, probable reports, absent testimony, and uncertain witnesses are expressly maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Probabilistic language is used for Peter and James, certainty for Paul's self-report, and uncertainty for the five hundred.

charity.alternative: The early list preserves genuine experiences even where surviving reports are indirect.
charity.decisiveQualification: Genuine underlying experiences would still leave historians without direct accounts or detailed verification for most named witnesses.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between an underlying experience and the historical quality of surviving testimony is explicit and consistent.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move identifies concrete source asymmetries, although its broader comparative-religion point is not developed in this span.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly establishes the central con requirement that appearance evidence be constrained by indirect testimony.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants probable experiences to several central witnesses while preserving the decisive source limitation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grants probable experiences to Peter and James, identifies Paul as direct, and notes missing testimony from Mary and the five hundred.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Christian appearance testimony is presented as stronger than Islamic or Mormon miracle claims because it involves multiple accepted witnesses rather than one founding visionary.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the discussion back to Justin, whose response directly contrasts the Christian witnesses with Muhammad and Joseph Smith.

components.text: Whether Christian attestation remains weak once directness and comparative cases are considered.
Whether multiple accepted witnesses distinguish Christianity from single-founder claims.
Whether the surviving accounts are direct and independent rather than merely numerous reports.

response.rationale: The response contacts the comparative demand by invoking several accepted Christian experiencers, but it does not resolve the objection that most surviving testimony is indirect.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive comparative component while leaving the directness and independence component unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move shifts between eyewitnesses, accepted experiencers, and testimonial sources without preserving those distinctions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A numerical witness contrast is asserted strongly despite the unresolved difference between reports about witnesses and extant testimony.

charity.alternative: Indirect but early reports about several experiencers may still cumulatively exceed a lone visionary report.
charity.decisiveQualification: That stronger reading still requires evidence that the reports are independent, direct enough, and accurately compared with the rival traditions.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Counting accepted experiencers does not by itself answer the distinction between multiple alleged witnesses and multiple direct attestations.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Christian count and claims about Islamic and Mormon attestation are asserted without adequate comparative documentation.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially supports comparative distinction, though it does not reach a central source-quality bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the comparative issue but presents the opposing source objection more weakly than its decisive form.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts four accepted Christian experiencers with Muhammad and Joseph Smith as allegedly solitary visionaries.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Mormon testimony concerning Moroni is presented as at least as directly documented and multiply attested as much New Testament appearance testimony, requiring consistent historical treatment.
moves.attributionBasis: The alternating exchange identifies Ehrman through his detailed correction about Mormon witnesses and his repeated appeal to impartial historical source evaluation.

components.text: Whether Mormon claims actually rest on only one relevant witness and are less directly attested.
Whether the Christian witness list contains surviving first-person testimony from Peter, James, and the five hundred.
Whether consistent comparative standards weaken the appearance component of the cumulative case.

response.rationale: The reply corrects the claimed numerical and documentary contrast, emphasizing extant Mormon testimony and absent first-person New Testament accounts, thereby defeating the stated comparison.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly identifies the faulty comparative premise and explains the consequence for impartial historical treatment.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison consistently distinguishes having a person's testimony from having a later report about that person.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The force is appropriately limited to comparative documentation and does not claim the Mormon event thereby occurred.

charity.alternative: The Christian traditions are earlier and may concern more independent experiencers than the Mormon case.
charity.decisiveQualification: Earlier dating and alleged multiplicity do not erase the absence of direct testimony from most named Christian witnesses.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The demand for the same evidential standard across traditions follows directly from the identified documentary comparison.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific testimonial asymmetries are identified, with only bounded compression concerning the exact Mormon documents and witnesses.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the subsidiary consistency bridge through an explicit cross-religious source comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly allows chronology to matter while retaining the decisive asymmetry in surviving direct testimony.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts extant Mormon testimony with the absence of testimony from Peter, James, and the five hundred.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Paul, Peter, and Mary were not expecting Jesus or a crucified Messiah to appear, unlike later believers already possessing categories for saintly appearances.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn continues Bass's first-person defense after the Marian comparison and names the apostles whose lack of expectation grounds his distinction.

components.text: Whether proposed religious parallels share the same absence of prior expectation as the first Jesus experiences.
Whether unexpectedness repairs the indirect character of most appearance testimony.

response.rationale: The move offers unexpectedness as a comparative distinction from later Catholic experiences, but it does not answer the source-access objection or the Mormon documentary comparison.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a secondary comparative issue but leaves the primary direct-attestation challenge substantially unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contrast is understandable, but the broad assertion that Paul, Peter, and Mary had no expectation lacks differentiated support.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The repeated claim that the first witnesses were in no way expecting an appearance exceeds the evidence supplied in the span.

charity.alternative: Some later Marian experiences may also occur without immediate personal expectation.
charity.decisiveQualification: A broader worldview permitting saintly appearances could still differ from expecting an individually resurrected Messiah.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Unexpectedness can distinguish cases, but it does not independently establish the veridicality of the unexpected experience.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The psychological expectations of several ancient individuals and later Catholics are asserted with little representative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move materially supports the subsidiary comparative-distinction bridge through the unexpectedness claim.

representationalCharity.rationale: The comparison is treated fairly enough, though variation among later visionaries is insufficiently acknowledged.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asserts that Paul, Peter, and Mary did not expect Jesus, unlike Catholics familiar with saintly appearances.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Unexpected Marian experiences show that lack of immediate expectation neither distinguishes the Jesus experiences nor establishes that the perceived figure appeared.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker challenges Bass's familiarity with Marian literature and repeatedly advances the skeptical comparison characteristic of Ehrman's preceding position.

components.text: Whether lack of immediate expectation uniquely distinguishes the first Jesus experiences from other religious visions.
Whether comparative religious experiences can occur unexpectedly despite an accommodating worldview.

response.rationale: The reply invokes unexpected Marian experiences and distinguishes expecting an experience from possessing a worldview that can interpret it, undermining the proposed uniqueness.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly attacks the decisive unexpectedness inference and states why surprise does not establish a real appearance.

precisionFindings.rationale: The core distinction is recoverable, although expectation sometimes shifts between personal anticipation and worldview possibility.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply appropriately argues that unexpectedness is nondispositive rather than claiming all cases are identical.

charity.alternative: A resurrection claim was less culturally available than a Marian apparition claim.
charity.decisiveQualification: That difference in interpretation does not show that the underlying experience was externally caused in either case.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference that surprise cannot distinguish veridical from nonveridical experience is clearly and consistently drawn.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Marian parallel is relevant, though representative details demonstrating genuinely unexpected cases are compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly attacks the subsidiary claim that unexpectedness distinguishes Christian appearances from parallels.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes the apocalyptic-worldview distinction and focuses narrowly on what unexpectedness can establish.

moves.evidenceBasis: The exchange distinguishes immediate expectation from a worldview allowing appearances and denies that surprise caused or verifies the event.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Initial followers could sincerely think they saw Jesus, after which apocalyptic Jewish embodiment beliefs could convert those experiences into the claim that God raised the Messiah.
moves.attributionBasis: After the moderator clarifies Bass's unexpectedness argument, Ehrman explicitly accepts the premise and develops his alternative account of how the belief formed.

components.text: Whether unexpected resurrection belief requires the followers to have expected Jesus to rise beforehand.
Whether sincere experiences plus apocalyptic interpretation offer a nonresurrection account of the novel claim.
Whether admitting that several followers thought they saw Jesus concedes a physical encounter.

response.rationale: The reply grants that followers did not expect resurrection, then replaces prior expectation with the historically relevant demand: how sincere experiences were interpreted within apocalyptic embodiment beliefs.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It preserves the legitimate unexpectedness issue while giving an explicit alternative route from experience to resurrection belief.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move carefully distinguishes thinking one saw Jesus, prior expectation, unknown additional experiencers, and later interpretation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The alternative is advanced as an available historical route while uncertainties about who experienced what are expressly acknowledged.

charity.alternative: The novelty of an individually risen Messiah may still demand more than generic apocalyptic belief.
charity.decisiveQualification: A sincere perceived appearance can provide the triggering datum that existing embodiment beliefs then interpret innovatively.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The sequence from sincere experience through culturally available interpretation to resurrection belief is explicit and noncircular.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The route fits the granted experiences and Jewish apocalyptic context, with some psychological and transmission details compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the central con bridge requiring a natural experiential and interpretive route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest novelty argument is granted, and the response explains rather than dismisses the resulting innovation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt grants that Peter, Mary, and Paul thought they saw Jesus while denying prior resurrection expectation and noting uncertainty about others.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Jewish followers had categories for exalted or disembodied survival until the final resurrection, leaving their claim that Jesus had bodily risen already as a novel development requiring explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator requests a quick response, and the resulting rebuttal defends Bass's established unexpectedness argument before the scheduled break.

components.text: Whether existing Jewish postmortem categories adequately explain the claim that Jesus was bodily raised already.
Whether an accommodating worldview makes the Jesus claim analogous to expected saintly appearances.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the cultural-interpretation route by naming available exaltation and final-resurrection categories, then arguing that neither yields an already bodily risen individual.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly addresses the decisive category question, though it does not fully exclude innovative recombination after an experience.

precisionFindings.rationale: Disembodied survival, exaltation, final collective resurrection, and Jesus's alleged present resurrection are clearly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The category contrast is supported, but the move implies explanatory inadequacy without comparing possible recombination or reinterpretation.

charity.alternative: Followers could innovatively combine appearance experiences with final-resurrection beliefs.
charity.decisiveQualification: That account must still explain why they asserted that one Messiah had bodily entered the final state ahead of everyone else.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The category contrast supports novelty, with only a bounded missing bridge from novelty to the need for resurrection itself.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The Maccabean and final-resurrection contrasts are specific, though the range of relevant Jewish interpretations is not surveyed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central pro claim that the immediate individual resurrection category was unexpected.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move allows existing categories but accurately emphasizes the qualification that the timing and individualization were novel.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts exalted disembodied martyrs awaiting final resurrection with the claim that Jesus had already risen bodily.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historians cannot treat an alleged one-time violation of physical law as the most probable explanation merely because a few people reported it.
moves.attributionBasis: The wording restates Ehrman's explicit objection about physical laws and contrasts historical probability with the reported claims of Paul and Peter.

components.text: Whether several historical reports can make a singular violation of physical regularity the most probable explanation.
Whether reports attributed to a few witnesses satisfy the evidential burden for the proposed event.
Whether novelty of belief independently raises the physical-event probability.

response.rationale: The reply attacks the cumulative inference at its methodological bridge: testimony from a few people does not by itself make an unprecedented physical exception historically most probable.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly identifies the probability defect in the inference, although it does not assess each cumulative component separately.

precisionFindings.rationale: The methodological proposition is clear, but 'law of physics' compresses distinctions among regularity, law, and supernatural intervention.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The base-rate point is strong, but the rhetoric risks treating unprecedentedness as nearly dispositive without specifying evidence thresholds.

charity.alternative: Exceptionally strong convergent evidence can rationally support a unique event.
charity.decisiveQualification: The presented reports must first be shown sufficiently direct, independent, and resistant to ordinary alternatives to overcome the extreme prior disparity.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The probability objection is coherent, though singularity alone cannot establish impossibility and requires an evidential-threshold bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Observed physical regularity and sparse testimony support the challenge, but no developed probability model or rival rates are supplied.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports the subsidiary historical-method bridge rather than directly completing the comparative motion route.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response leaves conceptual room for incredible evidence while finding the evidence presented far short of that standard.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts an alleged once-only violation across cosmic history with the reports attributed to Paul and Peter.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Appearances are only one component of the cumulative case, and the historical evidence is presented as consistent with what would be expected if Jesus rose.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker cites Bart's published formulation directly and uses the pro side's cumulative-case language about further evidence still to come.

components.text: Whether historical evidence can support resurrection despite the event's singular physical character.
Whether an ordinary interpretive route explains the same cumulative evidence at least as well.
Whether appearances are only one component rather than the entire evidential case.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the methodological objection by lowering the claim to cumulative consistency and stresses that appearances are only one line, but it does not compare explanatory probabilities.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the central consistency point while leaving the decisive comparative-probability demand largely unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The modest consistency claim is clear, though 'looks the same' leaves the relevant predicted observations insufficiently specified.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move appropriately retreats from proof or probability to consistency and attributes that limited concession accurately.

charity.alternative: The same evidence may also be consistent with ordinary experiences and later interpretation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Consistency with resurrection has little comparative force unless the evidence is more expected under resurrection than under those alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Cumulative consistency is coherent as a limited claim, but consistency alone does not establish comparative plausibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The cited concession supports compatibility, while the additional cumulative components and their likelihoods remain undeveloped.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly advances the motion-level cumulative-fit route, albeit with limited comparative force.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response fairly states the skeptical concession but does not fully engage its decisive comparative limitation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says appearances are one component and quotes the concession that existing evidence would be consistent with resurrection.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Historical conclusions compare probabilities, making ordinary misperception more likely than a unique physical exception even if supernatural intervention is abstractly possible.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly identifies what historians establish and repeats Ehrman's probability comparison between rare resurrection and common mistaken experience.

components.text: Whether mere consistency with resurrection makes it historically preferable to ordinary explanations.
Whether cumulative evidence overcomes the probability disparity between ordinary error and unique physical exception.
Whether cultural novelty changes the comparative base-rate calculation.

response.rationale: The reply identifies compatibility as insufficient and restores the comparative demand: historians must ask whether ordinary misperception is likelier than a unique physical exception.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly defeats the inference from consistency to plausibility by supplying the missing comparative-probability criterion.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction among possibility, consistency, and comparative probability is explicit and stably maintained.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The direction of the probability comparison is warranted, though the illustrative numerical disparity is not established in the span.

charity.alternative: A supernatural exception may be possible and the evidence may look as resurrection predicts.
charity.decisiveQualification: Abstract possibility and predictive compatibility do not show that resurrection outranks ordinary explanations on the available evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The comparative standard directly answers the compatibility claim without assuming that supernatural intervention is impossible.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Ordinary-versus-exceptional probability is well motivated, with a bounded gap in quantified rates and case-specific alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the con motion bridge requiring insufficient evidence to prefer a unique resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response expressly grants supernatural possibility for argument's sake and isolates the decisive comparative issue.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly contrasts historical probability, ordinary outcomes, and a conceded possible violation of physical regularity.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: Jesus's singular worldwide worship and divine status are presented as an extraordinary historical anomaly that makes the further extraordinary claim of resurrection more plausible.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the turn to Justin, and the speaker repeatedly frames the point as his own answer concerning Jesus's unique influence.

components.text: Whether extraordinary case-specific historical evidence can raise resurrection above its low prior probability.
Whether Jesus's unique influence supplies the incredible evidence demanded for a singular event.
Whether worldwide worship improves the direct quality of early appearance testimony.

response.rationale: The move contacts the probability objection by proposing Jesus's exceptional historical influence as case-specific evidence, but it does not establish a causal or likelihood link to resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It addresses the demand for extraordinary evidence while leaving the decisive inference from influence to physical resurrection unsupported.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical anomaly is clear, but worldwide worship and divine status are generalized without defined comparison classes.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Exceptional later influence is treated as making an earlier resurrection more plausible without a defended discriminating warrant.

charity.alternative: A singularly influential religious founder can acquire divine status through ordinary social and historical processes.
charity.decisiveQualification: The scale of later worship does not independently identify which causal process produced the founding belief.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from unparalleled influence to the physical truth of a founding miracle lacks a necessary causal bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Large-scale worship is asserted, but uniqueness, relevant comparison classes, and resurrection-specific likelihood are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly attempts to advance the motion-level cumulative plausibility claim through historical influence.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response notices the need for extraordinary evidence but underrepresents the strongest ordinary growth explanation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites billions worshipping Jesus as Lord and God and describes this as an extraordinary historical anomaly.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The number of people convinced that a miracle occurred establishes widespread belief but not the miracle, because movements acquire adherents for nonmiraculous reasons.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage states the skeptical distinction between proving belief and proving divine intervention, matching Ehrman's immediately preceding objections.

components.text: Whether the scale of later belief and worship provides evidence that the founding miracle occurred.
Whether subsequent spread supplies a resurrection-specific component of the cumulative case.
Whether widespread conviction distinguishes divine intervention from nonmiraculous belief formation.

response.rationale: The reply diagnoses the inference error: widespread conviction establishes the historical fact of belief, not the divine event believed, because movements grow for other reasons.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly identifies and defeats the decisive inference from adherent numbers to miracle occurrence.

precisionFindings.rationale: Belief, miracle occurrence, divine intervention, and nonmiraculous causes of conviction are cleanly distinguished.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical distinction is warranted: numbers directly establish conviction but cannot alone establish the event causing it.

charity.alternative: Extraordinary spread may be one probabilistic component rather than a deductive proof.
charity.decisiveQualification: It gains resurrection-specific force only if such spread is shown substantially more expected after a real resurrection than after sincere false belief.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between evidence of belief and evidence of the believed event is explicit and logically decisive.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant rests on a robust general distinction, though representative comparative growth cases are not supplied here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the central con bridge separating religious expansion from Jesus's physical fate.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response addresses the strongest probabilistic version by pointing to alternative reasons movements acquire adherents.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that many convinced people prove widespread conviction only and notes other reasons beliefs spread.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: The proposed evidence is not popularity alone but the improbable fulfillment of the specific worldwide mission attributed to the risen Jesus.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker explicitly corrects the preceding characterization, develops Bass's Moroni comparison, and returns to Jesus's worldwide mission.

components.text: Whether the argument depends merely on popularity or instead on fulfillment of a specific attributed mission.
Whether specific mission fulfillment materially changes the comparative probability of resurrection.
Whether the same evidential openness would be applied to a successful Moroni prediction.

response.rationale: The move justifiably replaces raw popularity with the narrower claim of an improbable mission prediction and professes symmetric treatment of Moroni, but does not establish attribution or predictive specificity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It preserves the legitimate growth issue and answers the replacement demand, though key fulfillment warrants remain compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction from popularity is clear, but 'all nations' and fulfillment are not operationally bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker calls fulfillment some evidence and allows analogous Moroni evidence, but understates attribution and selection concerns.

charity.alternative: Worldwide spread can fulfill a broad mission saying through ordinary missionary success.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Prediction fulfillment can be evidentially relevant, but the move leaves attribution, specificity, and causal connection partly implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The modern reach is observable, while the saying's dating, authorship, precision, and fulfillment threshold are not defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central pro expansion bridge by connecting growth to an attributed mission.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response correctly strengthens its claim beyond popularity while leaving the ordinary-fulfillment alternative live.

moves.proposition: The worldwide-mission saying comes through later Gospel authors, religious growth does not indicate truth, and incomplete global conversion undercuts the claimed fulfillment.
moves.attributionBasis: Bass directly addresses Bart, and the responding speaker states Ehrman's authorship position and consistently rejects the argument as theological rather than historical.

components.text: Whether a specific, attributable, and genuinely fulfilled mission prediction links Christian growth to resurrection.
Whether the religion's unusual growth indicates the truth of its founding claims.
Whether subsequent spread retains resurrection-specific cumulative force.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly attacks the attribution, evidential warrant, and fulfillment components of the mission argument.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The reply firmly denies resurrection-specific force while acknowledging the reported saying and historical expansion.

charity.alternative: Even a later Gospel source might preserve an authentic and remarkably fulfilled saying of Jesus.

representationalCharity.rationale: The strongest preservation possibility remains open, but its decisive historical requirements are accurately identified.

response.rationale: This is a constructive presentation of later vision reports, so it has no earlier opposing move requiring response contact.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Dreams do not establish that their objects are real, and analogous dream-appearance traditions in other religions contest the asserted uniqueness of Jesus visions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator invites Bart's view, and the responding speaker cites the Greek Asclepius tradition in a sustained skeptical historical comparison.

components.text: Whether dreams and visions reliably establish the continuing external activity of their apparent object.
Whether broad geographic spread makes religious experience uniquely truth-indicating.
Whether interpretive categories can generate sincere postmortem appearance traditions.

response.rationale: The reply separates having a dream from its object's reality and supplies the Asclepius tradition as a religious parallel, defeating the inference from report to unique agency.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly identifies the evidential defect and gives a concrete comparative case with the same relevant structure.

precisionFindings.rationale: The reply consistently distinguishes psychological experiences, external reality, and cross-religious uniqueness.

calibrationFindings.rationale: It argues that dreams do not establish reality and that parallels exist, without claiming every experience has one cause.

charity.alternative: Some Jesus visions may be unusually specific, transformative, or experienced by prior nonbelievers.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those features still require verification and comparison before they identify an externally active Jesus rather than generic religious experience.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between an experience and the independent reality of its object is explicit and decisive.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Asclepius supplies a concrete historical parallel, though the prevalence and detailed similarity of cases remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supplies the central con bridge explaining later Jesus visions through comparative religious phenomena.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply preserves the possibility of distinctive cases while accurately identifying their unmet evidential burden.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt denies that dreams establish their objects and describes Asclepius dream-healing traditions as an ancient parallel.

moves.speaker: Justin Bass
moves.proposition: The present worldwide pattern of Jesus visions, including reports from people previously unfamiliar with him, is distinguished from dormant ancient cult traditions as evidentially significant.
moves.attributionBasis: The speaker addresses Bart by name, challenges the Asclepius analogy, and returns to Bass's book research and named modern example.

components.text: Whether ancient cult dreams are sufficiently analogous to contemporary worldwide Jesus visions.
Whether worldwide distribution itself distinguishes truth from successful religious transmission.
Whether reports from people unfamiliar with Jesus overcome ordinary experiential explanations.

response.rationale: The response contacts the parallel by stressing contemporaneity and prior unfamiliarity with Jesus, but it supplies anecdotal assertion rather than comparative verification.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive similarity question but leaves ordinary mechanisms, documentation, and distributional comparison unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The contemporary distinction is recoverable, but hearing a voice, having a vision, and surviving an attack are evidentially blended.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The report is called powerful and generalized to definite worldwide cases without supplying verification or uncertainty controls.

charity.alternative: People previously unfamiliar with Jesus may have experiences not readily explained by prior Christian expectation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Prior unfamiliarity must be independently verified, and exposure, memory, reporting, selection, and cultural transmission remain live alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Prior unfamiliarity could be discriminating evidence, but the move lacks the bridge excluding exposure and reporting mechanisms.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: One vivid anecdote and asserted additional cases do not substantiate the claimed contemporary cross-cultural pattern.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central later-visions bridge by claiming a present cross-cultural pattern.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response identifies a potentially strong distinction but underdevelops the decisive alternative explanations.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt describes a man allegedly unfamiliar with Jesus who heard Jesus's voice and asserts that other such visionaries exist.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: Among the proposed facts, appearance reports supply the relevant historical evidence, but testimony from a few witnesses cannot establish an event contrary to consistently observed natural regularities.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator yields after Bart rejects a simpler characterization, and the speaker systematically evaluates Bass's five claims before stating his evidential standard.

components.text: Whether later cross-cultural reports can satisfy the evidential threshold for a resurrection contrary to regular experience.
Whether dreams and visions count as historical evidence of continuing external agency.
Whether the appearance material is the only component with direct historical bearing on resurrection.
Whether mission fulfillment constitutes historical evidence for Jesus's physical resurrection.

response.rationale: The reply evaluates the proposed lines, isolates appearances as relevant historical evidence, and argues that a few reports cannot overcome consistently observed natural regularities.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly attacks the later-vision inference and states the governing evidential consequence, while compressing the exact threshold.

precisionFindings.rationale: The evidential hierarchy is clear, though 'laws of physics' compresses physical regularity, methodological prior, and miracle claims.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The high threshold is warranted, but saying other lines are not historical evidence risks overstating their complete irrelevance.

charity.alternative: Cumulative indirect facts and numerous later reports may jointly raise the resurrection hypothesis beyond the first appearances alone.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those facts require resurrection-specific likelihood and reliable documentation before they can overcome ordinary explanations and strong regularity evidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The evidential-threshold argument is coherent, although a strong prior cannot by itself specify what quantity of testimony would suffice.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Stable natural regularities and sparse testimony support the threshold, with limited direct comparison of all reported cases.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly completes the con motion-level demand that the evidence remain insufficient to prefer physical resurrection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply considers the proposed lines systematically but somewhat understates their possible indirect probabilistic relevance.
